hints.hint: Announcement puzzles: build one list of complete scenarios, each also fixing every feature the problem leaves unstated — which quantity was made public, whether the two values may be equal, whether order matters. Drop scenarios violating the stated domain (natural number, exact division). Judge each statement only from that speaker's view: collect the scenarios matching what they see plus the value they hold; one match means they know, two or more means they don't. Never let a speaker use a fact you know but they were never told. So "I don't know" deletes exactly the scenarios where their own view was already decisive; apply statements in order and recount after each. Before answering, take each surviving scenario and replay every statement from both viewpoints, confirming each one is true there. If nothing survives, an unstated feature is still missing from your scenarios: add it and redo. Never fill the box with a plausible divisor or factor.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts (execution 149.138) scored 0: despite the incumbent's ban on global case splits, every rollout still opened separate 'sum' and 'product' cases, and inside the sum case argued that a holder of v immediately knows 2002-v, which credits the speaker with knowing the public number's role; four then declared the puzzle contradictory and boxed an arbitrary factor (143, 154, 13) while three burned the 16k cap looping. The revision replaces abstract 'recount jointly' language with two concrete steps the failures skipped: evaluate each statement strictly from that speaker's own view using only facts they were told, and replay every statement against any surviving scenario before answering, with an explicit widen-the-unstated-features rule instead of guessing when nothing survives.

hints.hint: To locate all roots on one circle or line, find one necessary condition, not the n roots. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Only then nth-root that scalar equation: |z-a| = k|z-b|, k^n = |c|; never apply the 1/n while nth powers still stand. k = 1 gives a line, their bisector. Else go straight to coordinates: z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 term, divide through by its coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius. Skip midpoint or diameter shortcuts; they invite sign errors. Radii are lengths, so a negative result just means a negative divisor: take its magnitude. That locus IS the answer; test one root at most. Report what is asked.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 round-7 rollouts scored 1, so training is saturated and the signal is token waste and transfer: the shortest, cleanest rollout (3.7k tokens, 6 hedges) ignored the incumbent's diameter-endpoints shortcut entirely and went straight to z=x+iy, square, divide by the x^2+y^2 coefficient, complete the square, while the four longest (5.1k-12.2k tokens, up to 37 hedges) all entered the endpoint/midpoint route early and only reached the coordinate route much later. The 12.2k outlier then stalled on two self-inflicted crises the endpoint route creates: a negative-looking radius from a negative 1-k^2 denominator (10 'negative' mentions) and applying the 1/n root while nth powers still stood. The revision therefore inverts the priority to make the coordinate route primary, explicitly drops the endpoint shortcut, and adds a portable rule that lengths are magnitudes so a negative expression is a sign of the divisor, not an error.

hints.hint: Union = areas summed minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Put the shared point at the origin. A corner there covers only a wedge: two half-planes whose boundary lines run through the origin. Those lines cut the interior of the other shape S, so part of S always lies on their far side, uncovered. Size never implies containment once a boundary crosses the interior: never set overlap to all of S, and skip tangency and origin-to-side distances. Decide membership only from the sign of each edge's linear form. If the origin is a k-fold rotational-symmetry center of S, the wedge angle is 2*pi/k, and both wedge edges leave S, then rotating by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and carries the wedge to the next position, so the k positions partition S into k congruent pieces and overlap = area(S)/k at every rotation. Compute that one area in the easiest orientation, report the union, and stop.
hints.subagent_summary: This round scored 5/8; all three failures collapsed the same way, asserting from extent alone that the 1x1 shape lies wholly inside the 2x2 one (one committed 4 outright, two burned the 16384-token cap oscillating between that containment claim and unsuccessful tangency/distance-to-side searches). The incumbent already forbids the containment claim but gives no checkable reason, so the student overrides the ban with a size argument. This revision supplies the mechanism: a corner covers only the intersection of two half-planes whose boundary lines run through S's interior, so some of S is necessarily outside, which makes extent-based containment self-refuting and keeps the rotation-partition proof that earned the best held-out score.

hints.hint: When each term of the required pattern may come from any of N given functions, never compare adjacent terms: neighbours can use different functions, so that route yields no bound, and a function's own index group need not be consecutive. Write the pattern's value at index n as an explicit T(n), then partition indices by which function produced them. On one function P's group, P - T vanishes and is not identically zero, since the low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term; so that group holds at most deg P indices. That cap is per group, hence Bound = N x deg P. Trust that product even if it looks too large for a contest. Verify once by construction: give each function its own block of consecutive indices and interpolate T there - free coefficients remain, so a legal function exists. Then finish immediately; re-opening a settled step or restarting the write-up runs out of space and scores nothing.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 public rollouts with the incumbent scored 5/8 and, unlike round 5, all three failures were token-cap truncations rather than wrong answers, so the fix must target looping, not aggregation. Two of the three re-imposed a constant step inside a single function's own values, concluded 'each function contributes at most one term', hit the contradiction with the hint's product, and oscillated until truncation; the third had already accepted the product and begun a clean final write-up but restarted the exposition and ran out of space. The revision therefore adds the one missing fact that kills the loop (a function's index group need not be consecutive, so its own successive differences carry no information) and a terminate-once-settled rule, trimming the verbose construction clause to stay under the token cap.

hints.hint: Kill a fractional base on sight: log_{1/k} u = -log_k u, so no later step depends on remembering the base is under 1. Each given point then reads u = k^{-y}, one linear equation in the parameters. A single vector equality between two sides is ONE constraint. Read the displacement straight off it; never re-derive it as equal diagonal midpoints or matching vertex sums, since that detour is where sign slips manufacture fake contradictions and burn the budget. Keep exactly one unknown: put a vertex at (t, f(t)), translate by that displacement, and force the image back onto the curve. The y-gap d becomes a single factor k^{-d} on the argument, leaving a rational equation in t. Drop roots repeating a known vertex or leaving the domain. Get each new vertex's y by evaluating f, not by adding the carried shift. Area = |cross product| of adjacent edges.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 public rollouts were correct (train_i=1.0), so train is saturated and transfer binds. The two most expensive rollouts (13360 and 10264 tokens) each spent hundreds of lines restating the single vector equality as equal diagonal midpoints or vertex sums; one of them derived a y-gap of 3 instead of 1 from that restatement and then wrote six passages about the problem being contradictory before recovering, while every clean short rollout took the displacement directly off the vector and never mentioned midpoints. Prior-round failures on this question had the same shape plus assigning a translated vertex a y from the carried shift rather than from f, so this revision replaces the base-under-1 warning with a one-line base flip that removes the direction trap outright, names the redundant-midpoint detour as the thing to skip, and keeps only the reduction lever, root filter, and evaluate-f rule.

hints.hint: Turn the requested event into a constraint on the sequence of moves, never into a symmetry claim: do not assume each item is equally likely to reach each position. Fix orientation once, since the earliest item placed on a pile stays at its bottom. Then see which steps the constraint forces and which are still genuine two-option choices; weight 1/2 per genuine choice and 1 per forced step, multiply along a sequence, and add the qualifying sequences.
hints.subagent_summary: This round scored 2/8; both successes converted the asked position into a requirement on which move happens last, then multiplied 1/2 only over the genuinely free binary steps, while five of the six failures used a uniformity shortcut (1/4 from 'each bag equally likely per position', 1/2, or 1/16 from 1/2^n) and one still claimed the order is forced. Rounds 1-6 show every rewrite longer than the 83-token incumbent lost held-out monotonically, so this proposal is deliberately near incumbent length and keeps only the one mechanism the successful rollouts used plus the orientation rule.

hints.hint: Read the unknowns as weights of a linear functional sampling distinct nodes; an exponent only labels which condition you are in, never a polynomial's argument. Any multipliers c_k applied to the given conditions and summed build a test polynomial p(t) = sum c_k t^k, and return sum_i a_i p(node_i) = the same combination of right-hand sides. So choose p to vanish at every node except the target one: that weight becomes a known number over a product of node differences. Use only exponents the conditions actually supply, evaluate the product at the target node instead of expanding it, and leave factorials closed-form.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts scored 0 (7 hit the 16384-token cap) with the same failure seen every round: each set P(x)=sum a_i x^i and reread condition k as P(k)=0, swapping the node with the condition exponent, then spent the budget on the resulting phantom free root and reported 1/2005, 0, 1/4008, -1/2004, or a harmonic sum. Six prior proposals at 132-184 tokens all lost heldout accuracy relative to the 82-token incumbent, roughly monotonically in length, so this round tests the untried short region: keep the incumbent's proven functional register and add only the one missing operational move, a combination of the given conditions forming a test polynomial that isolates a single weight.

hints.hint: Let N be the unstated count of identical units, and recover it from integrality rather than from the story: if every per-unit share must be a whole number, N divides each listed total, so the admissible N are their common divisors and the intended one is the maximum feasible count, namely their gcd. Before using any number from the text, say in words what that number counts; a count of groups, streets, rows, or batches is not a count of units, so it only forces N to be a multiple of it. Decide once whether each listed figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Then add all component amounts, divide by N, and apply any stated markup or discount as a single multiplicative factor; scaling and dividing commute. Finally check that every per-unit value is whole, that N meets all constraints, and that you reported the quantity actually asked for.
hints.subagent_summary: 6/8 public rollouts were correct and both failures shared one mode: they never mentioned gcd or maximality at all, instead lifting the stated group count directly as the unit count, dividing every listed total by it, finding each quotient whole, and treating that as confirmation. Rounds 5 and 6 attacked this by expanding the gcd machinery (front-loaded warning, maximality certificate) and both raised train while collapsing heldout from 0.2125 to 0.1125 and 0.0625, so more narrow divisibility apparatus demonstrably hurts transfer. Since lambda=5 I instead replaced the incumbent's near-vacuous grouping clause with a broadly portable quantity-labelling discipline - state in words what each given number counts before using it, and confirm you reported the quantity asked - which blocks the observed substitution without adding item-specific gcd steps.

hints.hint: If p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q the same degree n, do not grind the degree-n^2 coefficient system. Look for a common fixed point r and use the jointly centered form p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor that once as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A collapses to p=q. Let the given data, not a guessed sign, kill a branch. Then combine the conditions symmetrically instead of solving them one at a time: when two constraints differ only in the sign of one part, their sum kills that part and pins one unknown while their difference pins the other. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r and the identity at one spare point, then evaluate only the requested inputs in centered form, never expanding.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 public rollouts were correct again (8/8, 3.5k-5.7k tokens, none truncated), so the training question is saturated under the incumbent and every remaining point is transfer. Reading them, the centered ansatz and the factored both-branch condition are picked up verbatim and cause no trouble, but the incumbent's data step is stated only as a fact about this problem's two values ('their sum pins r, their difference pins A'), so rollouts treat it as a lookup rather than a method and several detour into re-solving the pair one equation at a time. This revision keeps the proven trigger, centered ansatz, branch derivation, and verification spine byte-identical and rewrites only that step as the portable rule that constraints differing in the sign of one part should be added and subtracted to decouple the unknowns, which should carry to unseen problems whose given data is not p(0),q(0).

hints.hint:
First pin down what ONE application is: the ENTIRE listed loop of sub-steps, each acting on what the previous produced. A single sub-step is not an application; count only completed loops. Check the loop runs over exactly the listed indices; never invent an extra sub-step.

Write the state as distinct labels and rewrite it fully per sub-step: swapping two adjacent length-L blocks trades them as rigid units carrying their current contents, tail unchanged. Confirm every label still appears once.

Never conclude "disjoint transpositions, so order 2": swapping length-L blocks is L parallel position swaps, and consecutive sub-steps share positions. Kill that story by applying the full loop twice and comparing.

Get exact counts for the smallest sizes. If a small case breaks the pattern larger cases set, suspect the small case and redo it letter by letter rather than answering piecewise. Once one larger size confirms a single clean formula, commit.
hints.subagent_summary: Only 2/8 correct; six failures shared two root causes. Several rollouts spent thousands of tokens unsure whether one application is the whole loop over k or a single block swap, then counted sub-steps as applications (one reported 3 for the 4-letter size, another invented a k=n sub-step that does not exist), and the rest collapsed a length-L block swap into one transposition and asserted order 2 untraced. Two length-capped rollouts had a small-size count that contradicted their own larger-size counts and concluded no single formula exists instead of redoing the cheap small case, so the revision defines the application boundary up front, guards the sub-step range, and tells the student to distrust the small case rather than go piecewise.
